items.article: Republican Sen. Josh Hawley and Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy are set to introduce bipartisan legislation that would hold AI companies legally liable for hacking incidents, as Google unveils its latest frontier model. Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., will introduce a bill alongside Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., that will hold companies civilly and criminally responsible if their AI agents go rogue and commit hacking incidents, Axios reported. Meanwhile, Google has announced its latest frontier AI model, Gemini 4 Argon. A viral exchange from this week's Senate hearing on rogue artificial intelligence is drawing fresh attention after Apollo Research CEO Marius Hobbhahn said a widely shared clip left out a key word because of a microphone issue. The clip appeared to show Hobbhahn warning Sen. Ruben Gallego that AI could be just "12 months" away from creating language humans cannot clearly understand. But Hobbhahn later said that was not what he intended to say. "This was totally my mistake," Hobbhahn wrote on X. "I said 'minus 12 months' as in 'already happened 12 months ago' but the mic only started picking up after the 'minus'. The subtitles picked it up, but I think it was barely audible." According to Hobbhahn, his point was that the milestone had already been reached roughly a year ago rather than being a prediction about what could happen over the next 12 months.

items.text: Why ‘Manchesterism’ May Face an Uphill Battle
items.article: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham wants to roll back decades of neoliberalism. Bloomberg Originals shows the hard choices coming amid a grim fiscal landscape. Margaret Thatcher’s tenure as UK prime minister ushered in one of Britain’s most significant economic transformations. When she took office in 1979, the nation faced severe economic stagnation, surging inflation and widespread industrial strikes during its so-called winter of discontent. Thatcher set about righting the economic ship while dismantling the post-war consensus, privatizing state-owned industries including utilities, restricting trade union power and deregulating financial markets. The Conservative’s policies triggered national turmoil, including deindustrialization, disempowerment of regional governments and high unemployment that earned her the ire of millions. But Thatcher’s policies remain in some form to this day. Now, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has pledged to break from her legacy. Speaking this week at a Labour Party conference, he outlined a new vision for the country, one including greater public control over key utilities and more regional power. In this Bloomberg Originals mini-documentary, we explore how Burnham might undo what Thatcher wrought — and the obstacles he faces in the attempt.

items.text: Donald Trump’s Approval Rating Shifts in the Midwest
items.article: President Donald Trump ’s net approval rating in the Midwest fell five points in a month as his national disapproval reached a second-term high in Emerson College Polling ’s series. It comes as Republican candidates in pivotal U.S. Senate races confront rural anger over fuel costs , the Iran war and a beef-import policy opposed by some cattle producers . Emerson's September survey found the Iran conflict, jobs and tariff policy were voters’ highest-ranked considerations when choosing a midterm candidate, with voters in Iowa, Kansas, Michigan and Ohio possibly determining whether regional dissatisfaction with Trump becomes a wider problem for the GOP . Trump-endorsed Iowa Republican Ashley Hinson has opposed increased beef imports and called for the Iran war to end while running for an open Senate seat. White House spokesman Davis Ingle previously told Newsweek that the 2024 election was the “ultimate poll,” saying nearly 80 million Americans had endorsed Donald Trump’s agenda. Ingle said the president had already made “historic progress” on jobs, inflation and housing affordability, and argued that further results would emerge as his policies took effect.

items.text: Walmart lighting up new feature for shoppers on digital price tags
items.article: Walmart shoppers can now use the app to activate a flashing light on electronic price tags to help locate an item on a shelf. If you've ever spent more than five minutes scrutinizing the spice options at the grocery store, Walmart has some exciting news for you. The retail giant said Thursday that shoppers can now use their mobile app while browsing in-store to activate a flashing light that helps locate items on shelves. The feature has been available for employees and Spark delivery drivers over the past several months, and is built into the new digital price tags appearing in Walmart's US stores for the past year. With the Walmart app — and its AI shopping assistant, Sparky — customers can search for the exact item they want and tap a button on the product listing page to activate a little green light in the aisle where they're standing. Business Insider saw the tech in action during a store tour in April, and a Spark driver said it has helped her fulfill delivery orders faster. The lights are also used by store employees to more quickly and accurately re-stock shelves, the company said.

items.text: What Tottenham must do in transfer window as major problems exposed
items.article: Spurs still lack quality and depth despite £300m summer spending spree Your weekly briefing on Tottenham, featuring team news and expert analysis from Sam Tabuteau I would like to be emailed about offers, event and updates from Evening Standard. Read our privacy notice . Tottenham have endured a nightmare start to the new season, sitting rock bottom of the Premier League table. Roberto De Zerbi ’s side are still winless after five frustrating top-flight games before the extended international break, despite spending in excess of £300million over the summer. Remarkably, given their lavish spending spree, Spurs still look short of quality and depth across the pitch, and it already feels like additions need to be made in January. Tottenham embarked on a full squad overhaul in the summer, bringing in 10 new players, and it is clear some are still finding their feet after a disrupted pre-season.
